'''''Quercus cerris''''', the '''Turkey oak''' or '''Austrian oak''',<ref>{{cite book |last1=Speer |first1=James H. |title=Fundamentals of Tree-Ring Research |date=2010 |publisher=The University of Arizona Press |location=Tucson |page=270}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Fonseca |first1=Matthew A. |title=The Measurement of Roundwood: Methodologies and Conversion Ratios |date=2005 |publisher=CABI Publishing |location=Wallingford, UK |page=242}}</ref> is a species of [[oak]] in the beech family ([[Fagaceae]]). It is native to southern and south-eastern [[Europe]], [[Asia Minor]], and the [[Levant]], but has been introduced outside its range. It is the [[type species]] of [[Quercus sect. Cerris|''Quercus'' sect. ''Cerris'']], a section of the genus characterised by shoot buds surrounded by soft bristles, bristle-tipped leaf lobes, and [[acorn]]s that usually mature in 18 months.

== Taxonomy and evolution ==
Turkey oak was [[Species description|formally described]] by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in his 1753 ''[[Species Plantarum]].''<ref>{{Cite web |title=Quercus cerris L. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:295941-1 |access-date=2026-09-03 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref> The species [[Botanical name|epiphet]] — ''cerris'' — derives from the Latin name for the species, ''cerrus'', which in turn may have come from a [[Root (linguistics)|root]] meaning 'hard',<ref>{{Cite web |last=Coombes |first=Allen |last2=Cameron |first2=Roderick |date=2021 |title=''Quercus cerris'' - Trees and Shrubs Online |url=https://www.treesandshrubsonline.org/articles/quercus/quercus-cerris/ |access-date=2026-09-03 |website=www.treesandshrubsonline.org}}</ref> or from a [[Berber languages|Berber]] term for oak.<ref>{{Citation |title=cerrus |date=2026-07-19 |work=Wiktionary, the free dictionary |url=https://en.wiktionary.org/w/index.php?title=cerrus&oldid=91653070 |access-date=2026-09-03 |language=en}}</ref>

Within the genus ''Quercus'', ''Quercus cerris'' is classified in [[Quercus sect. Cerris|section ''Cerris'']] of the [[Quercus subg. Cerris|subgenus ''Cerris'']], which is distributed in Eurasia, with a centre of diversity in the [[eastern Mediterranean]]. Within sect. ''Cerris'', Turkey oak is in turn classified in the subsection ''Cerris'', alongside ''[[Quercus castaneifolia|Q. castaneifolia]]'' and ''[[Quercus look|Q. look]]'', which are [[Endemism|endemic]] to the [[Hyrcanian forests]] and the [[Levant]], respectively.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Denk |first=Thomas |last2=Grimm |first2=Guido W |last3=Hipp |first3=Andrew L |last4=Bouchal |first4=Johannes M |last5=Schulze |first5=Ernst-Detlef |last6=Simeone |first6=Marco C |date=2023-04-11 |title=Niche evolution in a northern temperate tree lineage: biogeographical legacies in cork oaks (''Quercus'' section ''Cerris'') |url=https://doi.org/10.1093/aob/mcad032 |journal=Annals of Botany |volume=131 |issue=5 |pages=769–787 |doi=10.1093/aob/mcad032 |issn=0305-7364 |pmc=10184457 |pmid=36805162}}</ref>

After the [[Last Glacial Period|last glacial]], Turkey oak was restricted to areas south of the [[Alps]], however, fossil [[Gall|galls]] preserved at the site of [[Raalte]], the Netherlands, described in 2008, yielded indirect evidence that Turkey oak was present in [[northwestern Europe]] during the [[Last Interglacial|Eemian interglacial]] (130-115 thousand years ago), which preceded the last glacial.

At the site, two types of [[Oak apple|oak galls]] were discovered, one of which was clearly attributable to the [[Parthenogenesis|asexual generation]] of the [[gall wasp]] ''[[Andricus|Andricus hungaricus]]'', whereas the other type was more tentatively identified as belonging to the asexual generation of ''[[Andricus|Andricus quercusradicis]]''. Significantly, both ''Andricus'' species have lifecycles involving an asexual generation and a sexual generation, with each generation usually developing on a different host plant. With ''Andricus hungaricus'' in particular, the asexual generation is strictly restricted to [[Quercus subg. Quercus|white oaks]] (''Quercus'' subg. ''Quercus'' sect. ''Quercus''), ''[[Quercus robur]]'' in particular, while the sexual generation develops exclusively on cork oaks (''Quercus'' subg. ''Cerris'' sect. ''Cerris''), and especially on Turkey oak.

Importantly, these gall wasps therefore require the presence of oaks from both sections to complete their lifecycle, as evidenced by the invasion of several host-switching ''Andricus'' species (''[[Andricus corruptrix|A. corruptrix]]'', ''[[Andricus lignicola|A. lignicola]]'', ''[[Andricus kollari|A. kollari]], [[Andricus quercuscalicis|A. quercusscalicis]]'') into northwestern Europe in response to the [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalisation]] of Turkey oak in that area. Thus, although direct fossil evidence of Turkey oak during the Eemian of northwestern Europe is lacking, the galls preserved at Raalte imply its presence.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Van Der Ham |first=Raymond W. J. M. |last2=Kuijper |first2=Wim J. |last3=Kortselius |first3=M. ==Description==

''Quercus cerris'' is a large deciduous [[tree]] growing to {{Convert|25–40|m|abbr=off}} tall with a trunk up to {{Convert|2|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}} in diameter. The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is dark gray and deeply furrowed. On mature trees, the bark fissures are often streaked orange near the base of the trunk. The glossy [[leaves]] are {{Convert|7–14|cm|abbr=off|frac=4}} long and 3–5 cm wide, with 6–12 triangular lobes on each side; the regularity of the lobing varies greatly, with some trees having very regular lobes, others much less regular.

The [[flower]]s are wind-pollinated [[catkin]]s, maturing about 18 months after pollination; the [[fruit]] is a large [[acorn]], {{Convert|2.5–4|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long and 2 cm broad, bicoloured with an orange basal half grading to a green-brown tip; the acorn cup is 2 cm deep, densely covered in soft 'mossy' bristles from {{Convert|4–8|mm|frac=8}} in length.

== Distribution and ecology ==
First year acorns are very bitter, but are eaten by [[jay]]s and [[pigeon]]s; [[squirrel]]s usually only eat them when other food sources have run out.{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}}

The species' range extended to northern Europe and the British Isles before the previous ice age, about 120,000 years ago.{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}} It was reintroduced in the UK and Ireland in the eighteenth century as an ornamental tree,<ref>{{Cite news |date=2018-02-16 |title=The Definitive List of British Oak Trees & Their History {{!}} EHBP |language=en-GB |work=English Heritage Buildings |url=https://www.ehbp.com/the-definitive-list-of-british-oak-trees-their-history/ |access-date=2018-03-21}}</ref> its gall wasps now provide early food for birds.<ref>[https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/scotland/7566522.stm BBC News, " Ancient tree helps birds survive", 17 August 2008] Accessed 18 August 2008.</ref>
The tree harbours the gall wasp ''[[Andricus quercuscalicis]]'' whose larvae seriously damage the acorns of native British oaks. In 1998, the [[Ministry of Defence (United Kingdom)|Ministry of Defence]] ordered the felling of all Turkey oaks on its [[United Kingdom]] bases.

== Cultivation ==

Turkey oak is widely planted and is naturalised in much of Europe. This is partly for its relatively fast growth. It is used as an ornamental, and as a coastal [[windbreak]]. Several [[cultivar]]s have been selected, including 'Variegata', a [[variegation|variegated]] cultivar, and 'Woden', with large, deeply lobed leaves.

Turkey oak readily hybridises with [[cork oak]] (''Q. suber''), the resulting [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] being named [[Quercus × crenata|''Q.'' × ''crenata'']] <small>[[Jean-Baptiste Lamarck|Lam.]]</small> This hybrid occurs both naturally where its parents' ranges overlap in the wild, and has also arisen in cultivation. It is a very variable medium to large tree, usually semi-evergreen, sometimes nearly completely so, and often with marked [[hybrid vigour]]; its bark is thick and fissured but never as thick as that of the cork oak. Numerous cultivars are available, often grafted onto Turkey oak root stock. These include 'Ambrozyana', evergreen except in severe winters, originating from the Arboretum in [[Slovakia]], home of the late Count Ambrozy; 'Diversifolia', with the leaves extremely deeply cut leaving a narrow strip down the centre, and very corky bark; 'Fulhamensis' (Fulham oak), raised at Osborne's nursery in [[Fulham]] c.1760; and 'Lucombeana' (Lucombe oak), raised by [[William Lucombe]] at his nursery in [[Exeter]] {{circa}} 1762. An early specimen raised by Lucombe is at the [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.kew.org/visit-kew-gardens/explore/attractions/lucombe-oak |title=Lucombe oak |publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] |access-date=4 June 2006|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20141031091308/http://www.kew.org/visit-kew-gardens/explore/attractions/lucombe-oak|archive-date=2014-10-31 }}</ref> A similar Lucombe oak was felled by fungus and a light wind in Phear Park, [[Exmouth]] 15 February 2009.

== Cultivation and uses ==

The [[wood]] has many of the characteristics of other oaks, but is very prone to crack and split and hence is relegated to such uses as fencing.
